extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and advanced students interested in classical geometry and constructions (division of solids, ruled surfaces, elliptic-integral techniques)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedures and theoretical lemmas for dividing a given ellipsoid into n equal volumes (or into parts with prescribed ratios), plus supporting constructions for dividing a sphere and properties of ruled second-order surfaces used in such constructions. Contains multiple explicit geometric construction methods and prerequisite lemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem statement: divide a given ellipsoid into n equal volumes
rubrics_metrics.description: To divide a given ellipsoid into n equal volumes (or into parts having given ratios to one another).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the overall objective; the paper presents several distinct constructive methods (I–V, A, B, IV, etc.) and supporting lemmas to achieve it, and also gives methods for dividing the sphere which are used via correspondence to the ellipsoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method I — Wedge construction from dividing an ellipse
rubrics_metrics.description: Draw any diameter A'A of the ellipsoid and a diametral plane conjugate to it; the section is an ellipse. Divide this ellipse into n equal sectors P1OP2,...,PnOP1; through A'A and each line OPi let a plane pass; these n planes divide the ellipsoid into n equal wedges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth is evident because every plane section parallel to the diametral plane is divided into n equal sectors by intersections with the n planes. Applies equally to any finite portion cut off by parallel planes, and to hyperboloids, elliptic paraboloids, cones, and elliptic cylinders. Construction is geometric provided the ellipse can be geometrically divided into n equal sectors; otherwise the construction exists but may not be strictly geometric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma (a) — volume proportionality of cone-sector
rubrics_metrics.description: In a given diameter A'A, take point P; draw plane through P parallel to the conjugate diametral plane and describe from centre O a cone with the curve of section as director. The conical surface cuts off a solid sector which is to the whole ellipsoid as AP is to A'A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lemma gives the proportional relationship used to show divisions by cones based on division of the diameter; the paper gives an algebraic/volume argument relating cone, segment and sector volumes to deduce solid sector : whole ellipsoid :: AP : A'A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma (b) — proportionality between two conical cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: If through two points P and Q in diameter A'A planes are drawn and conical surfaces described as in (a), the portion of the ellipsoid included between these two surfaces is to the whole ellipsoid as PQ : A'A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify that dividing the diameter into proportional segments yields corresponding proportional volumes between the associated conical surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method II — Divide diameter and use concentric cones (cone construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take any diameter A'A, divide it into n equal parts, and through the n−1 division points draw planes parallel to the conjugate diametral plane; with centre O and the curves cut on the ellipsoid as directors, describe n−1 conical surfaces; these surfaces divide the ellipsoid into n equal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction is simple and general but requires describing cones of the second order, so it is not strictly geometrical in the classical sense. Also applies to portions of ellipsoid cut off by parallel planes. If the diameter is instead divided into parts having given ratios, the ellipsoid is divided into volumes having those ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method III — combine I and II for composite n (pq)
rubrics_metrics.description: If n is composite, n = p·q, divide the ellipsoid into p equal parts by Method I and into q equal parts by Method II using the same diameter; the mutual intersections of the p planes and q−1 cones divide the ellipsoid into pq equal volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining two independent constructions using the same diameter yields a finer subdivision when n is composite.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Solution A — sphere correspondence using great or small circles
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the surface of a sphere into n equal surfaces by arcs of great or small circles; find the corresponding curves on the ellipsoid; with these curves as directors and the ellipsoid centre as common vertex, describe cones; their mutual intersections divide the ellipsoid into n equal volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces the ellipsoid division problem to that of dividing a sphere and then mapping via the correspondence between sphere and ellipsoid surfaces. Use of small circles is allowed here but may preclude purely geometric constructions on the ellipsoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Geometrical Solution B — using only great circles (geometric mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the sphere into n equal surfaces by arcs of great circles; find the points on the ellipsoid corresponding to the angles of the spherical figures; join these points on the ellipsoid by straight lines in the same order as on the sphere; through each such straight line and the ellipsoid centre draw planes; these planes divide the ellipsoid into n equal volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excluding small circles makes the process geometrical on the ellipsoid. Note: if any great-circle arc used is a semicircle, the two diametrically opposite corresponding points are insufficient — an additional point in the semicircle must be taken to determine the corresponding ellipsoidal curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement: geometric feasibility depends on constructibility on sphere/ellipse
rubrics_metrics.description: A construction for dividing the ellipsoid is geometric only if the corresponding division of the ellipse (for Method I) or the sphere (for A/B) can be performed geometrically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly noted: some methods (e.g., those involving small circles or second-order cones) are not 'strictly geometrical' unless the auxiliary spherical/elliptical divisions are constructible by ruler-and-compass or equivalent classical construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere method 1 — inscribed polygon and meridians (divide into lunes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take any (great or small) circle on the sphere, inscribe in it a regular n-gon, and through the poles of this circle and each vertex draw planes that intersect the sphere in n semicircles (meridians); these meridians divide the sphere surface into n equal lunes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a straightforward way to obtain n equal spherical lunes; used as a building block for mapping to ellipsoid via A/B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere method 2 — divide diameter into equal parts (parallel-plane cuts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take any diameter of the sphere, divide it into n equal parts, and through the n−1 division points draw planes perpendicular to the diameter; these planes divide the surface into n equal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple construction; referenced to standard calculus/geometry texts. Can be combined with other sphere methods for composite n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere method 3 — combine (1) and (2) for composite n = p·q
rubrics_metrics.description: When n is composite (n = p·q), divide the sphere into p equal parts by method (1) and into q equal parts by method (2) using the diameter through the poles of the circle used in (1); intersections of great and small circles yield pq equal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to combining Methods I and II on the ellipsoid; useful for composite n where neither single method suffices elegantly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere method 4 — inscribe regular solid and project faces (limited set of n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscribe a regular polyhedron in the sphere and join its vertices by arcs of great circles in the order of the edges; this yields equal and regular spherical figures for n = 4,6,8,12,20 (and subdivisions thereof by further arcs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited applicability (only certain n corresponding to Platonic/Archimedean solids), but yields highly symmetric/geometric divisions; can further subdivide each face into isosceles spherical triangles to double number of parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere method 5 — nested spherical polygons in hemispheres (general constructive algorithm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide the sphere into two hemispheres and, in each, describe nested regular spherical polygons so that the mth polygon contains the preceding m−1 polygons; build polygons so that areas of annular regions are equal, yielding n equal surface areas overall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a constructive algorithm using polar triangles and spherical-triangle/polygon construction: for a regular spherical polygon of m sides with given area, construct the polar triangle and retrieve side lengths; choosing appropriate sequences of areas yields equal partitions. Works for general n and is the basis of General Geometrical Solution B when mapped to ellipsoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sphere method 6 — combine (1) and (5) for composite n
rubrics_metrics.description: If n = p·q, inscribe a regular p-gon in a great circle and use its poles and meridians (method 1) combined with nested polygon radii from method 5 to obtain q divisions along meridians, producing pq equal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extension for composite n combining symmetry in longitude with radial layered division; note if n is even the initial great circle plays the role of a small circle in counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability remark — most sphere methods adapt to spherical lune and ratio divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Most sphere methods (except method 4) can be adapted to divide a spherical lune into equal surfaces, and methods (1),(2),(5) can be modified to divide a spherical surface or lune into parts having given ratios instead of equal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This adaptability directly yields analogous constructions for dividing corresponding ellipsoidal wedges or solids into parts with prescribed ratios via the mapping to the ellipsoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method IV — trisection/arc-trisection construction (non-geometric except special cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Through a chosen diameter draw a circle KMLN with centre O and radius = A'A meeting A'A produced; divide KL into n equal parts P_i, erect perpendiculars meeting semicircle in Q_i, trisect arcs LNQ_i into R_i so that LR_i is one-third of the arc LNQ_i; from R_i drop perpendiculars to the diameter meeting it in S_i; through S_i draw planes conjugate to A'A; these planes divide the ellipsoid into n equal volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is simple and elegant but generally not geometrical because it relies on trisecting arcs (angle trisection). It yields segments whose successive differences are equal and thus equal volumes. Also adaptable to divide into prescribed ratios. For composite n it combines with Method I as in V.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method V — combine I and IV for composite n
rubrics_metrics.description: If n is composite n = p·q, divide the ellipsoid into p equal parts by Method I and into q equal parts by Method IV using the same diameter; mutual intersections of the resulting planes divide the ellipsoid into pq equal volumes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Another composite-number construction; note IV is typically non-geometrical (requires trisection), so the combined construction inherits that limitation where IV is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping principle: correspondence of points/curves between ellipsoids and spheres
rubrics_metrics.description: Given two ellipsoids (or an ellipsoid and a sphere) with equations in proportional form, points/curves on one correspond to points/curves on the other via fourth proportionals of coordinates: a point (x,y,z) corresponds to (d x, e y, f z) where proportions satisfy the ellipsoid equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a plane curve is given on one ellipsoid, the corresponding curve on the other is obtained by mapping three points and constructing the plane through their images; if the original plane passes through the centre the corresponding plane will too. This correspondence underlies General Solutions A and B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem (7) — proportionality of solid sectors cut by corresponding directors
rubrics_metrics.description: If corresponding closed curves on two ellipsoids are used as directors of cones with vertices at the respective centres, the solid sectors cut off by these conical surfaces are proportional to the volumes of the ellipsoids themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by covering the surface regions with infinitesimal corresponding triangular pyramids whose volumes scale by the same factor as the ellipsoids' volumes; this validates mapping sphere partitions to ellipsoid partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property of hyperboloid/ruled second-order surfaces — generatrix through a point on a directrix
rubrics_metrics.description: Given three directrices L, L1, L2 and a point p on L, construct the generatrix through p by drawing the plane through p and L1 and the plane through p and L2; their intersection is the generatrix through p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constructive description shows a generatrix arises as intersection of two planes each passing through the given point and one of the other directrices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property — plane sections of the hyperboloid of one sheet are conic sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Any plane section of the hyperboloid of one sheet that does not coincide with a generatrix or a directrix is a conic section.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by considering intersections of families of planes and showing the corresponding intersection points lie on a common conic; if the section-plane coincides with a directrix it reduces to two straight lines (possibly parallel if plane passes through the centre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property — cones from parallels to generating lines
rubrics_metrics.description: If lines are drawn parallel to all generating lines of either system of a hyperboloid, they constitute a cone (right or oblique); these cones are the same (for either system) if drawn through the same vertex point in space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma reduction: planes parallel to given families intersect in a line parallel to the original directrix; thus parallels to generatrices through a common vertex generate the same cone regardless of system chosen.
